lede: The heart is two pumps in one case: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side sends it round the body. Knowing which side, and which vessel, is most of the marks in this topic.
can: Name the four chambers and the four great vessels on an exam diagram.
Give the route of blood in order, and say why it passes through the heart twice.
Calculate a cardiac output and a percentage increase, and read a pulse trace.

text: The heart, double circulation and exercise

md: Put two fingers on your wrist and you can feel the heart working: about seventy squeezes a minute, every minute, for your whole life. It is two pumps in one case, side by side — and knowing which side sends blood where is most of this topic.

md:
The two upper chambers are the **atria**: they receive blood arriving from the veins. The two lower chambers are the **ventricles**: they pump it out again.

The **right** side handles blood coming back from the body and sends it to the lungs. The **left** side handles blood coming back from the lungs and sends it round the body.

prompt: Which chambers pump blood OUT of the heart?
explain: The ventricles. Atria receive, ventricles pump — which is why the ventricles have the thicker walls.

title: Why the pulmonary artery is an artery
md:
A vessel is an **artery** because it carries blood **away from the heart**, and a **vein** because it carries blood **towards** it. The blood inside has nothing to do with the name.

So the **pulmonary artery** is an artery even though its blood is deoxygenated, and the **pulmonary vein** is a vein even though its blood is oxygenated. Those two are the exceptions that prove the rule — and swapping them is the single commonest error in this topic.

prompt: Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
explain: The pulmonary artery. Away from the heart means artery, whatever the blood inside it is carrying.

prompt: Which ventricle is which in this photograph, and what does the difference in wall thickness tell you about where each one has to pump?

md:
Blood returning from the body arrives in the **vena cava** and works its way round in this order:

**vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta**

Nine names. Learn them as one sentence and every route question in the topic becomes a matter of starting in the right place.

prompt: Blood leaves the left ventricle through the ______.
explain: The aorta — the last vessel in the route, and the one Summer 2024's candidates most often could not name.

text: 4. A worked answer, start to finish

title: GCSE Biology Revision "The Heart and Circulation"
why: A short second pass over the route, now that you have the order in front of you.

title: Worked example: 'Stroke volume 70 cm³, heart rate 68 beats per minute. Calculate the cardiac output. [2]'
md:
**Step 1 — the equation.** cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. Multiply, because one stroke volume leaves the heart on every beat.
**Step 2 — substitute and evaluate.** 70 × 68 = **4760 cm³ per minute**.

The units settle the operation for you: cm³ per beat × beats per minute gives cm³ per minute. Adding the numbers would mean adding cubic centimetres to beats, which is not a quantity at all.

prompt: Your turn. During hard exercise her stroke volume is 110 cm³ and her pulse is 153. What is her cardiac output, in cm³ per minute?
explain: 110 × 153 = 16830 cm³ per minute — about 16.8 litres every minute.

md:
**Valves** sit between each atrium and its ventricle, and in the aorta and pulmonary artery where they leave. They shut against a backward flow, so blood can only go one way. **Coronary** vessels branch off the aorta and run over the outside of the heart, supplying the heart muscle itself.

Every organ has its own pair, named the same way: **renal** artery in and renal vein out for the kidney, **hepatic** artery in and hepatic vein out for the liver — plus the **hepatic portal vein**, which carries digested food from the intestine to the liver.

prompt: The vessel carrying digested food from the intestine to the liver is the hepatic ______ vein.
explain: Portal. It is the one vessel that runs from one organ's capillaries straight into another's.

md:
During exercise the muscles respire faster, so they need oxygen and glucose delivered more quickly and their carbon dioxide taken away. The pulse rises to move more blood every minute — here from 68 to 153, an increase of 125.0%.

Over **months** of regular exercise, two lasting things happen: the heart muscle is **strengthened**, and the **cardiac output at rest increases**. A stronger heart pushes more out per beat, so it can beat more slowly and still move more blood.

prompt: After months of training, what happens to cardiac output when at rest?
explain: It increases. The resting pulse falls, but the stroke volume rises by more — and increased resting cardiac output is the specification's own wording.
